newsitem.title: UK: EMS options vol curves reflect faith EMU to happen.
newsitem.headline: EMS options vol curves reflect faith EMU to happen.

text.p: Implied volatility curves for mark cross options are flattening as investors refrain from hedging what they now view as the fait accompli of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), options traders say.
The Finnish markka has even seen its volatility curve invert, so sure are investors that its entry into Europe's exchange rate mechanism is just a matter of time.
Risk reversals, which gauge the market's preference for calls or puts, are also growing less biased towards mark calls as convergence expectations increase.
"People are starting to back away from buying protection, which is what mark calls generally are," said a senior options dealer at a leading U.S. house in London.
One-month mark/Finnish markka volatility is currently quoted around 4.1/4.9 percent, with vol easing to 3.5/4.0 in one-year.
"There's a lot of speculation and hype about EMU entry and that's why back ends are getting smashed," said an options trader at a U.S. bank here.
For the French franc -- in the vanguard of currency union -- one-week volatility goes for 1.8/2.8 percent but thereafter all durations from one month out to one year are quoted at 1.9/2.4.
The mark's European satellites have made sharp gains in the spot market lately as confidence grows that European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will begin as planned in 1999.
The lira, for example, has strengthened beyond the key 1,000 per mark level as a market once dismissive of Italy's efforts to be in monetary union's first wave reconsiders.
But vols are not necessarily on a one-way street.

"If we start to see worries, if something concerns people about EMU progress, then all of a sudden customers will come in and start to hedge," said one dealer. "But in the current climate there's just no need."
That risk of upset was illustrated recently, when French president Jacques Chirac suggested Italy might not be among the first group of countries to form a single currency in 1999.
The lira swooped lower against the mark in response, easing below 1,000, although it soon rebounded. Chirac was outspoken but simply voiced what the market already knew, economists said.

"I think there is a degree of healthy scepticism in the market about Italy's ability, even after the budget, to get anywhere close to the Maastricht three percent (deficit to GDP) limit," said Robert Prior, European economist at HSBC Markets.
One-week mark/lira vols currently trade at 5.0/6.25 percent, rising to 5.2/5.7 for one month and 5.9/6.4 for one year.

Traders quoted risk reversals at around 0.4/0.6 percent in favour of lira puts. "That's still not a massive amount given that these things often trade at a full (1.0 percent) vol," said the senior U.S. bank dealer.
Risk reversals for mark/French franc options were even more narrowly in favour of mark calls, trading at 0.2/0.4 percent in the one-month area.
But here again market watchers counsel caution. All the good news for the mark crosses is now out, they say, and that poses the danger that risk reversals now firm for mark calls.
